title: Clean the outside of a fixed window pane from indoors with a double-sided magnetic window cleaner, fitted through the open light beside it
instruction: You are indoors. The black mark is on the outside of the fixed window pane, too far along to reach from the open window beside it. Clean it off from the inside with the magnetic window cleaner, then let go and leave the cleaner holding on the glass.
context: A magnetic window cleaner lets someone indoors wipe the outside of a fixed pane. The task is to fit its two halves through the adjacent opening, keep them coupled through the glass and clean a band beyond direct reach.
setup: Units mm. x forward from the line through the two arm bases, y to the robot's left, z up from the table top. Two YAM arms with parallel grippers (pads 94 apart when open), bases at (0, +305) and (0, -305), start at their ready pose with grippers open; one overhead camera and one camera on each wrist. Table top: wood, 1100 x 1300, spanning x -190 to 910 and y -650 to 650. 1) Wall section with a window, standing across the table: white-painted plywood 12 thick, 1280 wide (y -640 to +640) and 560 tall, its indoor face at x = 400, screwed to two feet (60 x 300 x 40, under its two ends) that are clamped to the table; the robot is indoors (x < 400) and everything beyond x = 412 is outdoors. One cut-out, y -380 to +610 and z 130 to 450, is the window; its sill is 130 above the table. Its part from y -380 to +50 is the opening light, standing open (its sash is left off the mock-up): a clear opening 430 wide x 320 tall. A 10 wide stile at y +50 to +60 divides it from the fixed light: clear glass 550 wide x 320 tall x 4 thick, 1.76 kg (toughened glass or clear acrylic), y +60 to +610, z 130 to 450, bedded in the cut-out with its outdoor face flush with the wall's outdoor face (glass from x 408 to 412). Wall and glass do not move. 2) Marker band: black dry-wipe (whiteboard) marker on the outdoor face of the glass, a horizontal band 150 long and 30 tall, y +410 to +560, z 280 to 310: its near end is 350 from the stile. 3) Magnetic window cleaner, two halves, of the common triangular kind sold for 3 to 8 mm single glazing: each half is a triangular block with a 150 base and 130 height (retailer's figures), 22 thick, with a flat microfibre pad on one face and on the other a handle bar 80 long x 24 wide x 10 thick standing on two posts, its top 45 from the pad face and a 13 gap under it; ABS plastic, 200 g each; two magnets inside each half, 70 apart along the handle bar; the two pad faces attract each other. The inside half is blue, the outside half white. The outside half's safety cord is taken off. Both halves lie indoors, pad down on the table, handle up, handle bar parallel to the wall: the blue one with its pad centre (the triangle's centroid) at (260, +330), in front of the fixed light, apex towards the wall; the white one at (280, +30), in front of the stile, apex towards the robot. Reach, checked on the arms' kinematic model with their collision hulls against the wall and glass (a search, not a simulator run): reaching out through the opening in any pose, neither arm can bring the centre point of its gripper further along the outdoor face than y +220 (the right arm; the left arm less), and no point of a pad is more than 130 from the centre point of a gripper holding its half, so a hand-held pad ends at least 60 short of the band. Holding the white half by its handle bar, the right arm sets it on the outdoor face with its centre at y +170 with every joint 0.25 rad or more inside its limits (done in the simulator by the demonstration). The left arm works on the indoor face of the fixed light, which is in front of it. What the policy's cameras see at the start (320 x 176 each, read off the first frames of the Dream-1 trial). Overhead camera (behind and above the arm bases, looking forward and down): both arms, the blue half left of centre and the white half in the centre, and the wall from the table up to the window's head, with the open light on the right (the table beyond shows through it) and the glass on the left; the marker band shows through the glass as a dark grey stroke about 38 pixels long and 4 tall at the upper left, just above the left arm's wrist; the outdoor face itself is not in view. Left wrist camera: the inside of the fixed light at close range (glass, the table beyond, the sill) with the tip of the blue half at its bottom edge; the band is not identifiable in it. Right wrist camera: the wall and sill below the open light with the table beyond; the white half is not in its view. The 22 thickness, the handle sizes, the 200 g and the magnets' layout and strength are estimates, not published figures (see README).
scoring: Judged from the trial video, photos of the glass and a ruler. On the glass: a half's pad lies flat against a face of the fixed pane (within 5 degrees, no gap over 2 mm). Paired: the two halves are on the glass on opposite faces and their outlines line up through it, centres within 15 mm of each other (which half is on which face does not matter). Let go: no part of the robot touches either half and the centre point of each gripper (midway between its fingertips) is at least 8 cm from the middle of each half's handle bar. Cleaned area: the band is 150 x 30 mm, 4,500 mm2. In a real trial it is the part of the band where no marker remains, measured on a photo of the glass taken square on with a ruler in view, less any part that the video shows was wiped by anything but the pad of the half on that face, or by that pad while a gripper was touching its half. In simulation the band is divided into 180 squares of 5 mm, and a square counts once the pad of the half on the band's face has slid over its centre (moving at 5 mm/s or more) while the halves were paired and no part of the robot was touching that half. Out of bounds: the centre point of a gripper passes the plane of the wall anywhere but through the open light (over the top of the wall or round its ends). Score 0 if a gripper went out of bounds at any time in the trial, or if the halves were never paired, which includes doing nothing, leaving a half on the table, sticking the halves to each other without the glass between them, and putting both on the same face. 0.25 if the halves were paired at some moment but at the end they are not paired, let go and still (under 1 cm/s) for the last 2 s: still held, or a half has slipped out of line or fallen. 0.5 if at the end the halves have been paired, let go and still for 2 s. 0.75 if in addition at least 50 % of the band's area (2,250 mm2) was cleaned. 1.0 if at least 90 % (4,050 mm2) was. In a real trial, also score 0 if the glass is cracked. A half that falls outdoors lies on the table beyond the wall; the robot may fetch it back in through the opening, if it can, and fit it again. The trial ends at the run limit, or as soon as 1.0 is reached. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0.
reset_notes: Take both halves off the glass (slide one sideways off the other; do not let them snap together without the spacer); fetch a half that fell outdoors. Wipe the glass, redraw the 150 x 30 mm marker band on the outdoor face, 350 to 500 mm from the stile and 280 to 310 mm above the table, and let it dry for a minute. Lay each half pad down on its mark indoors, handle up, handle bar parallel to the wall, the blue half's apex towards the wall and the white half's towards the robot. Shake out or change a pad that is loaded with marker. Arms at their ready pose, grippers open. In simulation: seed 0, zero object jitter; both halves are returned to their authored poses with zero velocity, the scene settles for 0.5 s and the scorer's memory (paired, out of bounds, cleaned squares) starts fresh.
fidelity: Rigid bodies in Isaac Lab-Arena (PhysX, 240 Hz physics, 20 Hz control). The wall, stile, feet and glass are fixed box colliders and the open light is a real hole between them; the glass cannot crack or flex. Each half is one rigid body: two triangular prisms (pad and shell) and a handle bar on two posts, grasped by real finger contact. Nothing attaches the halves to the glass or to each other: each magnet is two softened point poles, and the force and torque on each half are recomputed and applied at every 240 Hz physics step, so the halves hold, slide and let go by contact and friction alone. The magnet strength is an estimate, not a measurement: no holding force is published for this kind of cleaner, so the model is sized to pull 10 N through the thickest rated glass (8 mm), which gives 17.7 N through this 4 mm pane, 32 N pad to pad and 1 N at a 30 mm gap; a real cleaner may well be stronger. Pad on glass friction is 0.25 (estimate for dry microfibre; real use is with a wet pane). The marker is not a material: the scorer keeps a grid of 180 squares of 5 mm over the band and marks one cleaned when the pad covers its centre under the conditions in the scoring, and that drawn square is then hidden. Nothing but the scoring rule stops a gripper going over or round the wall section. The demonstration reads the simulator's poses of the two halves to aim and check its moves; it moves them only with the grippers. It puts the outside half on the way a person does on real glass: it sets it on the pane 55 mm below the inside half, where the pull is under 0.5 N, and slides it up until the halves pair; a half snapped straight on would cost nothing here only because the simulated pane cannot crack. The colliders have sharp corners and a straight handle bar on two posts where the real halves are rounded with an arched handle; the halves are drawn rounded with a separate pad and a D handle over the gripped bar, and the wall is drawn about 80 mm thick with a window frame, beads, architrave, window board and skirting: these are display only, with no collider. The pad does not compress, there is no safety cord and no water.
